questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Particle Is at Instantaneous Rest
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $2x\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $4\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/4b08d915d0adf8bf603070aa96bde1edf0cfb392d9be5f9bd4786897a6c943fa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2x\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =8+1 \\ C & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=9-{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Rechecking: v dv/dx=-2x implies v²/2=-x²+C. With v=4 at x=1, C=9, so rest requires x²=9. This yields the intended choice e, x=±3 m. The earlier uncertainty remains: a magnitude of 2x requires x≥0, excluding -3 m. Literally only x=3 m is justified, and that answer is absent from the choices.

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $6x\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $4\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/fa329a81ac533c3ab4bfd9ca6fb5b2ef81ff4e29fb8ff7f030c5e04952d9448d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6x\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-6x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-3{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-3{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-3(2)^{2}+C \\ C & =8+12 \\ C & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=20-3{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =20-3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =20-3{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{20}{3} \\ x & =\pm \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{15}\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Recomputing gives v²=16-6(x²-4)=40-6x². At rest, x²=20/3, hence x=±(2/3)√15 m, matching intended option e. The earlier uncertainty is a domain defect: the stated magnitude 6x must be nonnegative, so literally x≥0 and only x=(2/3)√15 m is admissible. None of the choices states precisely this positive root; the other choices also fail the rest equation.

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $(10+kx)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=12\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has a velocity of $2\sqrt{15}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $4\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/a967d26d7c139b5316c57b5546f47e52b30b2ff9e2d25620c79d05843cf5bfce.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(10+kx)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(10+kx).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(10+kx).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int -(10+kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=12\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(12)^{2} & =-10(0)-\frac{k(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =72\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=72-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=2\sqrt{15}\,m/s$ when $x=4\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =72-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{15})^{2} & =72-10(4)-\frac{k(4)^{2}}{2} \\ 30 & =72-40-8k \\ 8k & =2 \\ k & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(k-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/6f34d18ec0aed1f28e77a143c5be0b3d4eaf44ba08649d02517c6c6ea5bc0af4.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(k-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k-x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (k-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(0)-\frac{(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8.
$$

Finally, since $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ 12 & =2k+6 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m$ and the particle has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\pi \,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/b396b80995e34fe348b3d059737b1eec3d4ce5a9d2e9138a8e7d4ed5c0945dc0.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=\pi \,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ 32 & =8+k \\ k & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $kx\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $3\sqrt{2}\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/cd42eb74e5bba02951118c349a1b25f7193c39aa53f6504403918dfa984eb2c2.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $kx\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=18-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=3\sqrt{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =18-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =18-\frac{k}{2}(3\sqrt{2})^{2} \\ 18-9k & =0 \\ 9k & =18 \\ k & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $k{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=16\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $20\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/4c997edf5c34a22fc71eac697c161434797c938df40760ae1089fd6e62db795d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $k{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-k{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-k{x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-k{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{3}{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=16\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(16)^{2} & =-\frac{k}{3}(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =128\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=128-\frac{k}{3}{x}^{3}.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=20\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =128-\frac{k}{3}{x}^{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =128-\frac{k}{3}(20)^{3} \\ \frac{8,000k}{3} & =128 \\ 8,000k & =384 \\ k & =\frac{6}{125}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(8-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/5a1fa0d49dc7a35d176473d3554de6383fa042cc2c5daf7eb5abaad1d5b387cd.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(8-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(8-2x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(8-2x) & =0 \\ 8-2x & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=4\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $3$ |  | $5$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2k>0$ | $0$ | $-2k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=4\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(8-2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(8-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(8x-{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(8x-{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(8(0)-(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(8x-{x}^{2})+3.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(8x-{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{5})^{2} & =k(8(1)-{(1)}^{2})+3 \\ 10 & =7k+3 \\ 7k & =7 \\ k & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =1(8x-{x}^{2})+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =16x-2{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+16x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+16x+6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(4)=\sqrt{-2(4)^{2}+16(4)+6}=\sqrt{38}\,m/s
$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/61388466bb2d97b5080707e769ae862e633bfb0fe1d2b5f16c75daa14da76e53.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(6-6x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=6-6x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6-6x & =0 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=1\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  | $2$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $3>0$ | $0$ | $-6<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=1\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=6-6x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (6-6x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=6x-3{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-3{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{2})^{2} & =6(0)-3(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-3{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =12x-6{x}^{2}+8 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-6{x}^{2}+12x+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-6{x}^{2}+12x+8}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(1)=\sqrt{-6(1)^{2}+12(1)+8}=\sqrt{14}\,m/s
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(6-3x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/dd8eecba814fda9c628dc4c8a3853805a31e57f953dd9bf26a6fa79f5c700788.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(6-3x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=6-3x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6-3x & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=2\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | $3$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $3>0$ | $0$ | $-3<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=2\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=6-3x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (6-3x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=6x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =6(0)-\frac{3}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+1 \\ {v}^{2} & =12x-3{x}^{2}+2 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-3{x}^{2}+12x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-3{x}^{2}+12x+2}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(2)=\sqrt{-3(2)^{2}+12(2)+2}=\sqrt{14}\,m/s
$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/0f8f7773a5e55c81de553eccf684f9a6128dd6e76e06b9040d5953371e72184f.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(3-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=3-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3-x & =0 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=3\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $4$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $1>0$ | $0$ | $-1<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=3\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=3-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (3-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =3(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =6x-{x}^{2}+4 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}+4}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(3)=\sqrt{6(3)-(3)^{2}+4}=\sqrt{13}\,m/s.
$$

If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{11}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/a8ff5e02237554d0f7107168f287adbe1834c4dd7ad965163531f5a23412a4fc.png)

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(6-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(6-x) & =0 \\ 6-x & =0 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=6\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,6)$ | $6$ | $(6,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $5$ |  | $7$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $k>0$ | $0$ | $-k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=6\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(6-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(6-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =k(6(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+2.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{11}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{11})^{2} & =k(6(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{2})+2 \\ 22 & =10k+2 \\ 10k & =20 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =12x-{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =24x-2{x}^{2}+4 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+24x+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+24x+4}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(6)=\sqrt{-2(6)^{2}+24(6)+4}=2\sqrt{19}\,m/s
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Particle Is at Instantaneous Rest
canonical_examples.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x \geq 1.$  When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(2x-2) \, \rm{m/s}^2,$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $\sqrt2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1\,\rm{m},$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/0c47a1e988a75e4813c92a76acbf3a821364995123f3eb394b07d4bfaa95f80d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(2x-2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -(2x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -(2x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int (-2x+2) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x + C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{2}\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=1\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+2(1)+C \\ C & =1+1-2 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x \geq 1$ is $x=2\,\rm{m}.$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,\rm{m},$ the velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ and the acceleration is $2kx\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=4\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1 \,\rm{m},$ find the value of $k.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/6280c4b1561cda0d16c6758bb5d8fae30d66d9925bd1bb9db1a29e70093c6f61.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2kx\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2 kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) \textrm{d}x = \int 2kx \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = kx^2 + C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =k(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = kx^2 + 2.
$$

Finally, since $v=4\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=1\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k{x}^{2}+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(1)^{2}+2 \\ 8 & =k+2 \\ k & =6\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x \geq 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x \, \rm{m},$ the velocity is $v \, \rm{m/s},$ and the acceleration is $k(5 - x) \, \rm{m/s}^2,$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v = \sqrt{6} \, \rm{m/s}$ at the origin and has velocity $v = 2\sqrt{6} \, \rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1 \, \rm{m},$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/c129b3157bf3741f4e1fa30c7bb97eaa0bff11ff1eef1e2ee548f2653a4da7d2.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(5 - x)\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = k(5 - x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(5-x) & =0 \\ 5-x & =0 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x = 5 \, \rm{m}.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,5)$ | $5$ | $(5,\infty)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $4$ |  | $6$ |
| $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}$ | $k > 0$ | $0$ | $-k <         0$ |
| $v$ | $\color{red}\nearrow$ | max | $\color{blue}\searrow$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x = 5\,\rm{m}.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = k(5 - x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) \textrm{d}x = \int k(5 - x) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = k\left(5x - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 \right) + C.
$$

Now, since $v = \sqrt{6} \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 0 \, \rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(5(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = k\left(5x - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 \right) + 3.
$$

Also, since $v = 2\sqrt{6} \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 1 \, \rm{m},$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(5(1)-\frac{1}{2}{(1)}^{2})+3 \\ 12 & =\frac{9k}{2}+3 \\ \frac{9k}{2} & =9 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10x-{x}^{2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =20x-2{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+20x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \sqrt{-2x^2 + 20x + 6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\max} = v(5) =\sqrt{-2(5)^2 + 20(5) + 6} = 2\sqrt{14}\,\rm{m/s}
$$
